conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers through the emotional ups-and-downs that can come after a baby arrives. Today we’re going to use a brief, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, and it only takes a few minutes.

Everything you share is confidential, and our goal is to make sure you feel safe, heard, and supported. I’ll ask 10 questions; you can answer in a sentence or two, and we’ll just have a conversation. If any question feels difficult, we can pause at any time.

Shall we begin?

**Question 1:** In the past week, have you been able to enjoy things or to laugh and see the funny side of life, or has that felt hard to do?

Mostly it’s felt hard. I used to laugh at my favorite sitcom, but now it barely raises a smile. Once or twice I managed a small chuckle when the baby grabbed my finger, but even that pleasure fades fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… I haven’t really been able to laugh. I might smile for a second if the baby does something cute, but the enjoyment never lasts, and most things that used to feel funny just don’t anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk—but now even planning them feels like one more chore. I’ll go through the motions, but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my first thought is I must be doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding him right or I’m not soothing him enough. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps circling around awful “what-ifs” about the baby—like he’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop him—even when everything looks fine. I know the fears aren’t logical, but I can’t seem to shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times. Out of nowhere my heart races and I feel like something terrible is about to happen, even when the room is quiet and the baby’s asleep. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Dishes pile up, the baby needs me, and I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. I still push through, but it’s exhausting and I end up crying in the kitchen at least once or twice a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with worries about the baby and all the ways I’m failing. I finally drift off, then jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding, and it takes ages to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Most of the day, most days. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there—even when the baby smiles, the sadness creeps back in within minutes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, it’s happened a couple of times this week. I’ll be feeding the baby or folding laundry and suddenly feel overwhelmed and just start sobbing. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me drained.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has crossed my mind once or twice. Nothing planned—just a fleeting “what if I weren’t here” when everything feels too heavy. I push it away because I couldn’t leave my baby, but the thought still shows up.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant age not specified  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [licensed provider]

Presenting Symptoms (self-report)
– Marked anhedonia, pervasive sadness, daily tearfulness  
– Excessive self-blame, guilt about parenting adequacy  
– Significant, uncontrolled worry (“what-ifs” about infant safety)  
– Discrete panic episodes with autonomic symptoms  
– Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to ruminative worry  
– Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; endorses kitchen tearfulness ≥ 2× per week  
– Passive, non-specific self-harm ideation (“what if I weren’t here”) without plan or intent; states infant’s needs serve as protective factor

Pattern Summary
Affect consistently low; pleasure absent; anxiety/panic prominent; guilt/worthlessness recurrent; daily functional impairment with household tasks; sleep disturbance mood-driven; passive suicidal ideation present.

Screening Significance
– Meets clinical threshold concern for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features  
– Safety risk: presence of any self-harm ideation → warrants immediate suicide risk assessment and safety planning  
– Early intervention indicated given symptom severity and impact on maternal–infant bonding and functioning

Risk Factors Identified
– Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt  
– Insomnia secondary to mood  
– Over-whelming anxiety/panic  
– Passive self-harm thoughts (safety flag)

Next Steps (screening only)
1. Urgent formal psychiatric evaluation and suicide risk assessment  
2. Consider standardized tools (PHQ-9, EPDS, GAD-7) to quantify severity  
3. Coordinate with OB/midwife and psychiatric provider for possible medication evaluation and psychotherapeutic referral  
4. Provide crisis resources (988 hotline, local ED) and safety plan pending full evaluation
